clinicalPearls: ALS is the most common progressive motor neuron disease and ultimately causes progressive loss of BOTH upper (corticospinal) and lower motor neurons; in the absence of clear involvement of both motor neuron types, the diagnosis of ALS is questionable (p.3519-3520).

Lower motor neuron features: insidious asymmetric weakness usually first distal in one limb, progressive wasting/atrophy, and fasciculations (spontaneous twitching of motor units); in the hands a preponderance of extensor over flexor weakness is common (p.3521).

Upper (corticospinal) motor neuron features: hyperactive muscle-stretch reflexes (tendon jerks), spastic resistance to passive movement, and muscle stiffness often out of proportion to weakness (p.3521).

Bulbar onset presents with difficulty chewing, swallowing, and moving the face and tongue; corticobulbar degeneration causes dysarthria and pseudobulbar affect (involuntary excess weeping or laughing) (p.3521).

World Federation of Neurology criteria: simultaneous upper AND lower motor neuron involvement with progressive weakness and exclusion of all alternative diagnoses; 'definite' when 3-4 regions involved (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral), 'probable' when 2, 'possible' when 1 (p.3521).

Elevated CSF/serum neurofilament light chains (Nfl) or phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chains are markers of neurodegeneration in most cases; higher levels correlate with more aggressive disease and more rapid progression (p.3521).

About 10% of cases are inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (familial ALS); FALS is clinically indistinguishable from sporadic ALS apart from its inheritance. C9orf72 is the most common genetic cause (~45-50% of FALS), followed by SOD1 (~20%) (p.3521).
ALS may arise concurrently with frontotemporal dementia (particularly in familial cases), with early behavioral abnormalities reflecting frontal lobe dysfunction (p.3520-3521).
harrison.pathophysiology: Motor neuron degenerative disorder marked by death of lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells and their brainstem bulbar homologues) and upper/corticospinal motor neurons (layer-five motor cortex neurons descending via the pyramidal tract). Affected neurons shrink and accumulate lipofuscin; the motor neuron cytoskeleton is affected early, with proximal axonal 'spheroids' composed of neurofilament accumulations. Both sporadic and familial ALS show ubiquitin-positive aggregates frequently associated with the protein TDP43, plus astroglial/microglial proliferation (neuroinflammation). Loss of cortical motor neurons thins the corticospinal tracts; lateral-column fiber loss and fibrillary gliosis impart firmness (lateral sclerosis), while muscle denervation and atrophy give rise to the term amyotrophy. Neuronal cell death is strikingly selective: the sensory apparatus, cerebellar coordination structures, ocular-motility neurons, and the sacral parasympathetic sphincter neurons (nucleus of Onuf) are characteristically spared. Familial ALS most commonly involves mutations in C9orf72, SOD1, TDP43, and FUS/TLS (p.3519-3521).
additionalDifferentials: Cervical spondylosis / compression of the cervical spinal cord or cervicomedullary junction (tumors, foramen magnum lesions, osteophytes)
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMCB)
Diffuse lower motor axonal neuropathy associated with hematopoietic disorders (lymphoma, multiple myeloma) with serum M-component
Primary lateral sclerosis (upper motor neuron only)
Progressive muscular atrophy (lower motor neuron only)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy / structural compressive lesions (parasagittal or foramen magnum tumors, Chiari malformation/syrinx, spinal AVM)
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (treatable - responds to IVIG or chemotherapy)
Plasma cell dyscrasias and motor neuropathy with paraproteinemia or cancer (paraneoplastic)
Metabolic: hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia; deficiency of folate, vitamin B12, vitamin E, copper or zinc
additionalInvestigations: MRI of head including foramen magnum and cervical spine to exclude compressive structural lesions
Electrophysiologic testing (EMG/nerve conduction) to demonstrate denervation and to detect motor conduction block (suggests MMCB rather than ALS)
Serum/CSF neurofilament light chains (Nfl) - prognostic marker of disease aggressiveness
Complete blood count, sedimentation rate, total protein, anti-GM1 antibodies (should be obtained in all cases)
Anti-Hu antibody (paraneoplastic), serum protein for M-component, bone marrow biopsy if indicated
Fasting blood sugar, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12/E/folate, serum zinc and copper
WBC DNA for mutational analysis (C9orf72, SOD1, TDP43, FUS/TLS) in suspected familial cases
Contrast myelography to visualize the cervical cord where doubt exists
redFlags: Respiratory involvement: weakness of the muscles of respiration may rarely cause death before the disease is advanced elsewhere; the illness is relentlessly progressive, leading to death from respiratory paralysis - respiratory failure determines prognosis.
Bulbar dysfunction (difficulty chewing/swallowing) risks aspiration pneumonia and compromised nutrition/hydration.

Atypical features warranting search for a remediable mimic: restriction to only upper OR only lower motor neurons, involvement of non-motor neurons, or evidence of motor conduction block on electrophysiology.
harrison.prognosis: Relentlessly progressive; median survival is 3 to 5 years, with death typically from respiratory paralysis. Stabilization or regression is very rare. Higher serum/CSF neurofilament light chain levels correlate with more aggressive disease and more rapid progression. No treatment arrests the underlying pathologic process (p.3521, 3524).
pitfalls: Because ALS is currently untreatable, it is imperative to exclude potentially remediable mimics - especially cervical cord compression/cervical spondylotic myelopathy, which can produce weakness, wasting, fasciculations in the arms and leg spasticity that closely resembles ALS.

Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMCB) must be excluded: unlike ALS it lacks corticospinal signs, often has elevated anti-GM1 antibodies, and may respond dramatically to IVIG or chemotherapy.
Diagnosing ALS without clear involvement of BOTH upper and lower motor neurons is questionable - reconsider the diagnosis.

Features favoring ALS over a compressive mimic: absence of pain or sensory changes, normal bowel and bladder function, and normal spinal radiology and CSF. Sensory, sphincter, ocular-motility, and cognitive functions are preserved even late (except when concurrent frontotemporal dementia is present).
harrison.severityClassification: World Federation of Neurology diagnostic categories based on number of body regions with combined upper and lower motor neuron involvement (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral): 'definite' ALS = 3-4 regions; 'probable' = 2 regions; 'possible' = 1 region. Exception: progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs at one site plus a SOD1 mutation also qualifies (p.3521).
management: Offer the glutamate modulator riluzole to slow progression, and edaravone in appropriate patients
Support respiratory function with non-invasive ventilation as respiratory muscle weakness develops, and manage airway secretions
Maintain nutrition with dietetic input and timely gastrostomy feeding when dysphagia threatens safe swallowing and intake
Treat symptoms specifically, using antispasticity agents such as baclofen, anticholinergics or botulinum toxin for sialorrhoea, and treatment for pseudobulbar affect and cramps
Provide communication aids and mobility and functional equipment as weakness advances
Manage within a multidisciplinary motor neuron disease clinic with early palliative care and advance care planning
Offer genetic counselling and family screening in familial disease such as C9orf72 or SOD1 mutations
